name: Waray / Waray-Waray, Samar-Leyte Bisayan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Zorc, R. David. 1977. The Bisayan dialects of the Philippines: subgrouping and reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44. Canberra: Australian National University. doi:10.15144/PL-C44 (open access). Waray-specific corroboration: Oyzon, Voltaire Q., Firie Jill T. Ramos & Michael Carlo C. Villas. 2011, rev. 2016. An Bag-o nga Ortograpiya han Winaray, sec. 5 'An stress, o accent'; Romualdez, Norberto. 1908. A Bisayan grammar.. Takloban, pp. 2-3 'The accents'.
catalog_quote: [Zorc 1977 p.216, 8.10] All Bs speech varieties except some dialects of Kuy and Tsg retain phonemic accent. The following minimal pair is found in all dialects and establishes contrastive accent for PBS: púnuq [pú:nuq] tree trunk < PBS *púnuq and punúq [punúq] full < PBS *punúq. [p.218, 8.10.2] (1) CANONICAL FORM. In all Bs dialects studied, a closed penult is stressed. Thus, stress is predictable from the shape of the form: all dialects síŋsiŋ ring < PBS *síŋsiŋ, all dialects búkbuk weevil < PBS *búkbuk. Regardless of the accent on the base form, if morphophonemic changes produce a form with a CVC-penult, the penult is stressed. [p.50, 3.1.3, acutes dropped by scan] The vowel in an accented open penult (CV) is long: all dialects (but Kuy and Tsg) bataq → [ba:taq] young. The vowel in an unaccented (CV) or closed (CVC) syllable is short ... In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult [CVC.CV(C)] are accented on the penult (see 10.2.1.). In all dialects stress is a syntactic feature, a means of counting the full words in a clause, informing the hearer how many full words the speaker utters; it does not always coincide with length. [Oyzon, Ramos & Villas 2016 sec. 5] An stress, o accent. ... Pananglitan: susô (fresh water snail), susò (tightly knit), susó (breast) ... An laton nga may istruktura nga CVC ug hikakagian san-o an kataposan nga laton han termino permi mayda “accent” o, “stress”, Pananglitan: bag-o, ándam

new_statements.rule_in_words: Waray (like all Bisayan varieties Zorc surveyed except some Kuyonon/Tausug) has lexically contrastive word accent: a root is accented either on the penult or on the ultima, unpredictably for open penults (minimal pairs such as púnuq 'tree trunk' vs punúq 'full'); an accented open penult is realized with vowel length; if the penult is closed (CVC) the penult is always stressed, including in derived forms. Waray-specific sources corroborate this first-hand: Romualdez 1908 pp.2-3 (acute accent 'located wherever it is needed', upa vs upa), Oyzon, Ramos & Villas 2011/2017 sec.5 (contrastive accent, non-final length = accent, CVC pre-final syllable always stressed: bag-o, andam), KWF [2018] pp.62-66 (stress distinguishes meaning; túbo vs tubó, súka vs sukà, sálog vs salúg).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Zorc p.50 notes a secondary accent on the antepenult in some dialects and (p.245) that antepenult vowel length, lost in most Bisayan, 'can freely occur in dialects of the Masbate, Sorsogon, and Waray areas' (e.g. N-S na:ka-báyad 'can pay'); Oyzon et al. 2017 note words with two accented syllables (mákaón).
new_statements.exceptions: Closed (CVC) penults are always stressed regardless of the base accent; historically an *ə (>u) in an open penult pushed accent to the ultima (púnuq-type vs punúq 'full'); verb/stative accent pairs (tápus 'to finish' : tapús 'finished', incl. War examples); pronouns, deictics, interrogatives and numerals 1-9 tend to ultima stress (S-L examples p.69); stress placement can be overridden by emphatic/exclamatory intonation while length remains.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical accent in citation forms; Zorc separates length (lexical, on accented open penult, never on the ultima) from stress, which 'is a syntactic feature.. it does not always coincide with length' and can shift under intonation (p.50-51). Statement is pan-Bisayan from Zorc's own fieldwork, explicitly including Waray sample points War, S-L, N-S.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding quote (Zorc 1977) is a pan-Bisayan first-hand statement covering all 36 Bisayan speech varieties Zorc surveyed, which explicitly include three Waray sample points: 'War' (Waray, southern/eastern Samar), 'S-L' (Samar-Leyte, central Waray incl. Leyte) and 'N-S' (Northern Samar). The Waray-specific corroborating sources describe standard (Tacloban/Leyte-Samar) Waray: Romualdez 1908 = Samareño-Leyteño 'Bisayan' of Tacloban; Oyzon, Ramos & Villas 2011/2017 and KWF [2018] = standard written Waray (with notes on Eastern Samar schwa dialects). All fall under wara1300; no separate dialect glottocode asserted.

sources.citation: Romualdez, Norberto. 1908. A Bisayan grammar and notes on Bisayan rhetoric and poetics and Filipino dialectology. Takloban: Pag Pahayag Co. (Samar-Leyte Bisayan = Waray)
sources.note: 'THE ACCENTS' pp.2-3: a vowel 'pronounced.. with more force than others in the same word' takes the acute; 'The acute is located wherever it is needed, either at the beginning or in the middle or at the ending of the word' (upa 'reward' vs upa 'rice chaff'; quita 'we'/'see'/'look at'); grave/circumflex mark final glottal without/with force. I.e. accent is lexically contrastive; later sections give accent-shift rules under suffixation (penult vs last syllable).
